summary: Provides a problem statement and gap analysis for IP-based autonomic networking. It reviews what exists for self-management and where current network management depends too heavily on central control.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist of what is missing before networks can run themselves, compared with todays tools.

questions: what is missing for self-managing networks
how do networks manage themselves today
subtitle: What networks still need to manage themselves automatically

tldr.problem: Most aspects of network management require manual configuration and human administrators, even though routing already demonstrates autonomic behavior.
tldr.mechanism: This gap analysis compares what aspects of networking are already automatic or autonomic with areas that still depend heavily on humans and centralized management systems.
tldr.outcome: It identifies missing features like device coordination, reusable components, secure control planes, and knowledge sharing that autonomic networks would need.

today: RFC 7576 remains an informational gap analysis that identifies the problem and missing features. Work on autonomic networking has continued in the IETF through standards like RFC 8342 (YANG), but comprehensive autonomic networks with all the features described remain research and early deployment.

sections.title: The Vision of Autonomic Networks
sections.content:
The fundamental goal of an Autonomic Network is self-management: the network configures, optimizes, heals and protects itself without human intervention. Routing protocols like OSPF and IS-IS already do this. However, most other aspects of networking—address management, security setup, performance tuning, troubleshooting—still require top-down configuration by human administrators.

This RFC proposes that all network configurations should work like routing: automatic, distributed, and self-adapting. Rather than eliminate human administrators, the goal is to free them from tedious, error-prone tasks like manual IP address entry and repetitive configuration checks, leaving them to focus on high-level decisions and complex troubleshooting.
sections.plainLanguage: A self-managing network would be like a car that fixes itself when something breaks. Routing protocols already do this, but most of networking still needs a person to decide every detail.

sections.title: What Is Already Automatic
sections.content:
Networks already have some automatic features. DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to hosts instead of requiring manual entry. Router advertisements in IPv6 let hosts automatically find their default gateway. DNS servers can be discovered automatically instead of manually configured. Routing protocols dynamically calculate paths and adapt to failures. NTP synchronizes time across the network without central control.

These examples show that automatic, distributed decision-making works in networks. The RFC notes that some security mechanisms like IEEE 802.1x and BGP Flowspec also show autonomic properties, allowing systems to adapt after authentication or when threats are detected.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks already have autopilot in some places: IP addresses assign themselves via DHCP, routers find routes automatically, and time syncs across the network. These work because they let devices talk to each other directly.

sections.title: What Still Requires Humans
sections.content:
Building a new network requires humans to analyze needs, choose hardware locations, design the topology and the security model, and configure every device manually. Network maintenance still depends on human administrators who design service templates and respond to new customer requests. Configuration errors are common because decisions rely on human intelligence or rigid templates.

Security setup typically requires detailed human intervention to decide password rules, firewall policies, VPN configurations and cryptographic choices. Troubleshooting and recovery still depend on humans to diagnose failures—although networks could autonomously switch traffic around failures and even predict device overloads before they occur, they do not do so today.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, humans have to think about every detail: deciding where routers go, writing security rules, and fixing problems when something breaks. Templates help but they are rigid and often wrong.

sections.title: The Missing Pieces
sections.content:
Autonomic networks need several missing features. First, they need better device coordination: devices must understand their dependencies and resolve them locally instead of relying on a central script. They need to discover neighbors, synchronize network status, and negotiate changes with each other. Second, they need reusable protocol components for identity, security, messaging and service discovery, rather than each protocol inventing its own.

Third, they need a secure control plane for autonomic operations to communicate safely without requiring a central management system. Fourth, protocols should have better defaults and less configuration. Many existing protocols offer endless options for corner cases; autonomic networks would pick sensible defaults or decide parameters automatically based on what neighbors are doing.

Finally, networks need forecasting and knowledge sharing. A network could test changes in a "dry run" mode on the control plane before applying them to live traffic. It could learn from history, reuse configurations that worked in similar networks, and use analytics of current conditions to make better decisions autonomically.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks would need to talk to each other to coordinate, to trust each other securely, to have sensible defaults instead of hundreds of options, and to learn from what worked before.

sections.title: Security and the Path Forward
sections.content:
This gap analysis does not describe new security threats—it is about identifying what is missing before autonomic management is feasible. However, it emphasizes that autonomic technology must be designed with strong security from the start, since a network with vulnerable autonomic functions would be at great risk. The control plane for autonomic operations must be secure against forged commands and man-in-the-middle attacks.

The RFC acknowledges that some aspects of network management will always require human decision-making, such as business policies and high-level design choices. The aim is not to automate everything, but to shift tedious, routine, error-prone work to autonomic functions so humans can focus on complex decisions and oversight.
sections.plainLanguage: If networks manage themselves, they have to be really good at not accepting fake instructions. Some decisions will always need a person—business policy, strategy, and hard calls. But the boring stuff can be automated.
